client: I've been really struggling lately with how much is piling up at work. My boss just dumped two new projects on me with these insane deadlines, and I already felt like I was barely keeping my head above water at the marketing agency. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change the fact that I have way too much on my plate right now.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now, and I can hear the tension and urgency in how you're describing it — like you're already stretched thin and now the weight just got heavier. That feeling of "what's the point of talking when the pile doesn't shrink" makes complete sense, and it's actually worth noticing that thought, because sometimes our mind convinces us that nothing can help right when we need support the most. Let's not try to make the pile disappear today, but see if we can find a way to help you feel a little less alone under it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I guess that's a fair point — my brain does kind of go to "this is hopeless" pretty fast. But I still feel like even if I feel less alone, I'm going to go back to my desk tomorrow and the deadlines are still going to be staring me in the face. It's hard to separate the emotional stuff from the practical reality of just having too much work.
therapist: Your voice is telling me something important right now — there's a real urgency and tension underneath your words, even if you're framing things pretty calmly, and that gap makes sense when you're bracing for tomorrow. You're absolutely right that the deadlines are real, and CBT isn't about pretending they aren't — it's about asking whether the story your brain adds on top, like "this is hopeless" or "I can't handle this," is actually helping you tackle them or just making the weight heavier. What if we looked at what's actually on your plate and separated what's truly urgent from what your mind is catastrophizing about?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Okay, I can see the logic in that, but honestly when I try to sort out what's "truly urgent" versus what I'm catastrophizing about, it all feels urgent to me. Like, both of these new projects have real deadlines from my actual boss, not just ones I invented in my head. I guess I'm worried that if I try to reframe it as catastrophizing, I'll just end up minimizing something that actually needs my full attention.
therapist: That's a really important distinction you're making, and I want to validate it — you're not catastrophizing the deadlines themselves, those are real, and your concern about not dismissing them shows how conscientious you are. The reframe isn't about minimizing what's urgent, it's about noticing whether the *feeling* that everything must be handled perfectly and all at once is helping you work, or just exhausting you before you even start. Sometimes the most practical thing we can do is separate "this deadline is real" from "and therefore I'm going to fail" — the first is a fact, the second is a story worth examining.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually makes a little more sense to me — I think I do jump pretty quickly from "this is a lot of work" to "I'm going to drop the ball and my boss is going to think I'm incompetent." But even knowing that's a story I'm telling myself, I'm not sure how to stop it from feeling completely true in the moment when the pressure is on. Like, how do I actually catch myself doing that when I'm already in the middle of a stress spiral?
therapist: I can hear how activated you are right now even as you're working through this thoughtfully — there's a real urgency in your voice that tells me this isn't just an abstract question for you, it's something you're feeling in your body right now. That's actually the perfect place to start: when you notice your pitch rising, your thoughts speeding up, that physical sense of pressure — that *is* the signal, and you can train yourself to use it as a cue to pause and ask "what story am I adding right now?" It takes practice, but even just naming it in the moment — "there's that spiral" — creates a tiny bit of distance between you and the thought, so it loses just a little of its grip.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I like the idea of just naming it — "there's that spiral" — because it feels simple enough that I might actually remember to do it. But I'm a little skeptical that in the middle of a really bad moment at work, like when my boss is standing over my shoulder asking for updates, I'm going to have the presence of mind to pause and do that. It feels like the stress just kind of takes over and I'm running on autopilot before I even realize what's happening.
therapist: There's something telling in how you're speaking right now — your voice is soft but moving quickly, like part of you is already rehearsing that stressful moment even as you describe it, which makes your skepticism completely understandable. You're right that in the thick of it, you won't have time to philosophize — so the goal isn't to catch the spiral perfectly, it's just to practice naming it *after* the fact at first, maybe even that evening, so your brain slowly starts recognizing the pattern earlier and earlier over time. Think of it less like a skill you need to nail under pressure right away, and more like building a muscle that gets faster with repetition.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Okay, doing it after the fact feels a lot more manageable than trying to catch it in real time — I think I could actually do that. But I'm a little worried that by the end of the day I'm going to be so drained from work that I won't want to reflect on anything, I'll just want to zone out and not think about it at all. That's kind of my default when things get really hard — I just shut down and distract myself, which I know probably isn't helping.
therapist: There's something worth noticing in how you just described that — your words feel a little deflated, like you're already anticipating the shutdown before it's even happened, and that tiredness comes through even as you're speaking quickly and working hard to think this through. The zoning out isn't a character flaw, it's actually your mind's way of protecting itself from overwhelm, but you're right that it tends to pause the processing rather than resolve it. What if the "after the fact" reflection didn't have to be deep or effortful — just one sentence in your phone, like "I spiraled today when my boss asked for updates" — something so small that even an exhausted, checked-out version of you could manage it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: One sentence in my phone actually sounds doable — I think the reason I always resist this kind of stuff is because I imagine it turning into this whole journaling exercise that I'll inevitably fail to keep up with. But I guess I'm also a little worried that I'll write the sentence and then just feel like I'm documenting how stressed I am without actually doing anything about it, like it becomes this record of all my bad days. Does just noticing it really move the needle, or is it more of a stepping stone to something else?
therapist: There's something quietly vulnerable in the way you're asking that — your voice is soft and a little tentative, like you're genuinely hoping this isn't just busywork but also bracing for disappointment, which makes a lot of sense given how drained you already are. Noticing *is* the first real step, not just symbolically — because you can't interrupt a pattern you can't see yet, and that one sentence starts building the awareness that eventually lets you respond differently in the moment rather than just document the spiral. Over time, the log stops being a record of bad days and starts becoming evidence that you *survived* them, which is actually pretty powerful data against that story that you're going to drop the ball.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe — thinking of it as evidence that I survived rather than just a list of failures — actually hit me a little harder than I expected. I think part of why the work stress feels so overwhelming is that I genuinely don't give myself credit for the fact that I've gotten through hard stretches before, I just move straight on to the next thing that's going wrong. I'm going to try the one sentence thing this week, but I'm also a little nervous that if I miss a day or two I'll just use it as proof that I can't follow through on anything, which is kind of its own spiral.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in the way you just said that — your voice is soft and a little high, like something genuinely landed for you, and that mix of openness and worry feels very real. What you just named *is* the spiral in miniature — your brain is already pre-loading a missed day as proof of failure before you've even started — so here's the reframe: missing a day isn't data about your follow-through, it's just a missed day, and coming back after missing one is actually stronger evidence of resilience than a perfect streak. So the rule isn't "don't miss," it's "always come back" — which is a much more forgiving game to play with yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

You came into this conversation skeptical that talking would help, and you're leaving with something you want to try — that's not someone who doesn't follow through.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
